paras: The threatened lynching of Henry Granel occurred on the evening of October 25, 1888, at Sheepshead Bay, Long Island, New York, when villagers threatened to lynch a hotel keeper arrested for striking a teenage jockey with a baseball bat. Police held the crowd back with drawn revolvers and took Granel to a cell at Coney Island, and no one was killed. Daily papers treated the assault as a notably brutal crime, while weekly digests reported that Granel had been "narrowly saved from lynching."

Henry Granel was described as the proprietor of a small hotel in the village, a middle-aged man weighing 190 pounds. According to the longer dispatch, he was "a perfect fiend" when drunk, which it called "a not unusual occurrence." No paper stated the race of Granel or of anyone else involved.

At about 8 o'clock on Thursday evening a 17-year-old jockey named Brown, weighing eighty pounds, entered the hotel while Granel was intoxicated. In the longer account, Granel became angry during a conversation and struck Brown, the boy hit back, and Granel then seized a baseball bat and struck him on the head, felling him to the floor. The short dispatch described only an "altercation" and said the boy was knocked senseless and "seriously injured."

Granel then turned on the bystanders, who fled. They found a policeman, Rem Williamson, who according to the dispatch agreed to act only after they had "threatened dire vengeance." Once Williamson arrested Granel, the crowd "talked loudly of Lynch law," and the villagers threatened to lynch him. A second policeman, Garrison Morris, took charge of the prisoner, drew his revolver to hold the crowd back, and took Granel to Coney Island, where he was locked in a cell.
No later report of Brown's condition, or of any charge, hearing or trial for Granel, appears in the coverage.

The story first ran on October 27 in two forms datelined Sheepshead Bay. The Richmond Daily Times printed a short version under "Knocked Senseless with a Base-Ball Bat," while the Annapolis Evening Capital carried a longer one headlined "Beaten by a Brute" that called the assault "one of the most brutal crimes ever committed on Long Island." The Camden Evening Telegram ran the same longer text that day as "The Deadly Base Ball Bat," and the Essex County Herald in Vermont reprinted the short version on November 2.

The longer dispatch condemned Granel as a "would be murderer" but was also dismissive of the crowd, calling it "the mob, characteristic of its name." A condensed item in weekly news digests reversed the emphasis, reporting that Granel had been "narrowly saved from lynching by the indignant villagers" and calling the injured boy "a stripling." That item ran between November 1 and 3 in at least six weeklies, including papers in Mississippi and Missouri, where the man's name appeared as Garnet, Gravet, Granet and Graner.

The two dispatches spelled the accused man's name Granel, while the weekly digest printed it as Henry Garnet, with further variants in reprints. The dispatches, closer to the event, also supply the details the digest omits, including the boy's name and the policemen involved.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Henry Granel
bases: Villagers threatened to lynch an arrested man and officers drew revolvers to hold the crowd back; no one was seized or killed, so this is a threatened lynching (A1, A2, A4).
The crowd threatened lynch law against Granel for an alleged assault, but police kept it back and took him to a cell; no one was killed (A1, A2, A4).
Two differently worded Sheepshead Bay dispatches agree on the assault, the lynching threat and the police holding the crowd back with revolvers (A1, A2), though both may trace to one news source.

accounts.label: Short wire dispatch (Oct. 26)
accounts.gist: Granel, drunk, felled the jockey Brown with a bat during an altercation; the villagers threatened to lynch him and the arresting officers drew revolvers to keep the crowd back.

accounts.label: Longer dispatch (Oct. 27)
accounts.gist: Granel struck Brown first, Brown hit back, and Granel then used the bat; bystanders fled, a reluctant policeman made the arrest, the mob talked of lynch law, and a second policeman held it off with a revolver and jailed Granel at Coney Island.

accounts.label: Weekly news digest
accounts.gist: On the 25th 'Henry Garnet' was narrowly saved from lynching by indignant villagers for striking 'a stripling' with a bat; police drew revolvers to keep the crowd at bay.

framing.detail: Headlined 'Beaten by a Brute' and 'Little Jockey Brown Assaulted by a Drunken Hotel Keeper', it condemned Granel as 'a perfect fiend' and 'would be murderer' while calling the crowd 'the mob, characteristic of its name'.
Headlined 'Knocked Senseless with a Base-Ball Bat', a short factual dispatch.
Digest item framed the crowd as 'indignant villagers' and the blow as 'murderous', without comment on the lynching threat.
The longer dispatch ran in Camden as 'The Deadly Base Ball Bat', the short one in Vermont, and the digest item in at least six weeklies.

conflicts.note: Granel is the spelling in both dispatches; the digest's Garnet and its reprints' Gravet, Granet and Graner look like typesetting or OCR variants. The dispatches are the closer source.

versions.value: Granel struck Brown first; Brown retaliated before the bat blow

conflicts.note: Not a contradiction; the longer dispatch gives more detail.
